title: Evaluate a Postfix Expression

concept.title: Postfix: operators come after their operands
body: In **postfix notation** (also called reverse Polish notation) an operator is written **after** its two operands: `3 4 +` means 3 + 4, and `2 3 4 * +` means 2 + (3 * 4). There are no parentheses and no priority rules, which makes postfix easy to evaluate with a stack.

Read the tokens from left to right. A **number** is pushed. An **operator** takes its two operands from the top of the stack (the first one popped is the **right** operand), computes, and pushes the result.

Mind the order for `-` and `/`: it is `a - b`, not `b - a`. Division of integers rounds **towards zero** (`7 / 2 = 3`, `-7 / 2 = -3`). C++ and Java already do this; in Python use `abs` and fix the sign, because `//` rounds down.

statement: Evaluate an expression in postfix notation. The tokens are integers (possibly negative) and the operators `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. Division of integers rounds towards zero. The expression is valid and never divides by zero.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, the number of tokens.
The second line has the `n` tokens separated by spaces.
outputFormat: Print the value of the expression.
constraints: Every number and every intermediate result has an absolute value of at most 10^15.
hints: An operator pops two values; the first popped is the right operand.
The result is the only value left on the stack.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
t = input().split()

explanation: Numbers are pushed; an operator pops its right and left operand, applies the operation and pushes the result. The single value left is the answer.
